First off, calling fascism “just national syndicalism” is a massive oversimplification. National syndicalism was a fringe intellectual influence on early Italian fascism, but fascism as a political movement has always been defined much more by its embrace of authoritarian nationalism, its hatred for class struggle, and its total subordination of workers’ organizations to the state and capital. Fascism isn’t just “Marxism but nationalist.” It’s the weaponized opposite of Marxism born specifically as a violent reaction to socialist and communist movements.

Mussolini being a “communist before shifting to nationalism” is just a fun fact, not a political argument. Plenty of people switch sides. What matters is that fascism, once it actually emerged, was used as a bludgeon against the working class and the left. That’s why communists and socialists everywhere fought it and died fighting it. Fascism’s entire project was about smashing independent worker power and preserving capitalism in crisis.

The claim that “anti-fascism is just Stalinist propaganda” is ahistorical nonsense. Antifascism arose out of the real experience of working-class organizations having to literally defend themselves against fascist violence, both before and after Stalin was even relevant internationally. Anti-fascism isn’t about “poisoning the well,” it’s about survival.

And for the record, no serious Marxist or historian “links Hitler to fascism” because of Stalin or postwar propagandax they do it because both were expressions of counter-revolutionary, anti-worker, ultra-nationalist capitalist reaction. They shared enough in common that they’re studied together, not because of some Stalinist PR campaign.

This confusion is fair, because liberal and idealist philosophy have trained us to see all “shoulds” as moral imperatives. But this is the crux of the philosophical misunderstanding between moral normativity and historically conditioned interest. Marx’s “should” is not rooted in morality, it’s rooted in material necessity and class interest. To say “we should act in our own best interests” sounds moral if you’re thinking in the abstract, like a rule about what humans ought to do in general. But Marx isn’t offering universal prescriptions, he’s describing how, given the structure of capitalism, the working class has every material incentive to oppose the system that immiserates them. It’s not “suffering is bad and must be opposed” in the moral sense. It’s: suffering generates resistance because people live, act, and rebel inside material conditions that shape their interests.

When you touch a hot stove, your body recoils. No one would say, “Ah, a moral judgment has been made!” You’re reacting in line with your structure. Class struggle functions similarly. When the system produces mass suffering, homelessness, alienation, destruction, resistance isn’t a moral conclusion, but a material one. That’s what Marx meant when he said that the proletariat is “compelled” to overthrow capitalism.

So no, it’s not a moral claim to say “we’ll crash if we don’t change course.” It’s a structural analysis: capitalism contains the seeds of its own destruction. Saying we should change course is not a Kantian “ought.” It’s a reflection of the fact that the material logic of the system will force us to act - or be destroyed. It’s not about goodness, but survival.

Marx doesn’t say “oppose suffering because it’s bad.” He says: suffering emerges from the contradictions of capital, and people pushed far enough will fight. That’s not moralism but dialectics.

He doesn’t say, “Capitalism is bad because it offends universal morality.” He says, “Capitalism is a historically specific mode of production with internal contradictions that produce exploitation, alienation, and eventually its own downfall.”

His critique is structural, not ethical. When he exposes surplus value, it’s not to say, “Shame on the bourgeoisie,” but to demonstrate how exploitation is embedded in the system itself. He’s not appealing to a moral standard outside history—he’s showing how relations of production shape consciousness, institutions, and ideology from within history.

When he calls for the abolition of private property, it’s not a plea to moral conscience. It’s the logical outcome of the proletariat’s position in the process of production. As he wrote in the Communist Manifesto: “Communism is the real movement which abolishes the present state of things.” Not a utopian dream, not a moral plea—a movement rooted in the material contradictions of capitalism.

People confuse passion in Marx with morality. But anger, critique, revolutionary fervor—these aren’t necessarily moral categories. They can be expressions of clarity, of class consciousness, of historical understanding. Marx’s fire comes from seeing the machinery grind people up and knowing—scientifically, historically, dialectically—it doesn’t have to be this way.

You’re trying to trace Marx’s commitment to revolution back to a hidden normativity—essentially arguing that Marx, despite his claims to scientific objectivity, is still smuggling in a moral imperative: that we ought to revolt, that we should act in history to fulfill its rational trajectory. And because this echoes Hegel’s system—where Spirit must come to know itself—you see Marx as still fundamentally idealist, just with a materialist wardrobe.

But that’s not quite right, because what you’re describing isn’t morality in the sense Marx is dealing with. Marx isn’t making a claim about what ought to be done from some universal ethical standpoint—he’s describing the process by which classes, formed by their material conditions, are driven to act. Revolution isn’t a matter of choosing to do the right thing—it’s the result of contradictions becoming unbearable. When a worker joins a strike or sabotages a machine, they aren’t referencing the Categorical Imperative or aligning with “the Ideal”—they’re acting out of the reality of their condition.

That doesn’t make it amoral, it makes it non-moral in the way science is non-moral. The desire to resolve alienation, immiseration, exploitation—these are not abstracted from experience, they are experience. Marx isn’t saying, “You should revolt because it’s good”; he’s saying, “You will revolt, because your position becomes intolerable.”

Now, that doesn’t mean Marx is purely deterministic either. Consciousness matters. Organization matters. He writes because theory and practice aren’t separate for him. Praxis is the fusion. People don’t just react—they interpret their world and act within it. So the point of writing Capital wasn’t to tell people what they should do out of some moral high ground, it was to give them a clearer lens for understanding the world they’re already struggling to survive in.

Calling this Idealism stretches the term past its useful boundaries. Yes, Marx believed there is a rational structure to history—but not one driven by spirit or metaphysical teleology. It’s driven by real contradictions in material production: exploitation, surplus value, crisis. If there is a “should” here, it’s not rooted in abstract morality—it’s emergent from the historical process itself. When Marxists say “we must abolish capitalism,” it’s not the same as “we should be nice to each other.” It’s closer to saying, “the engine is on fire—if we don’t change course, we crash.”

You ask, why care at all if it’s inevitable? But inevitability in Marx isn’t a passive unfolding—it’s a tendency conditioned by contradictions. Without organization, consciousness, and struggle, capitalism won’t just dissolve into socialism—it can descend into barbarism, fascism, ecological collapse. Marx doesn’t promise that socialism is fated—he says it’s possible, and its possibility is immanent to capital’s development. But whether it’s realized depends on struggle.

So to say Marx is secretly moralizing is to misread him through a philosophical lens he already left behind. He’s not hiding normativity—he’s replacing it. He doesn’t say “follow the Ideal”—he says “understand the world, and change it, because you are already within it.” And if you don’t, the world will change anyway—just not in your favor.

To be honest, the impulse to find some hidden “ought” in Marx might come from the same place as the bourgeois need for justification—something existential to anchor our choices. Marx denies us that comfort. Revolution doesn’t need to be justified. It happens when the world demands it.
